title: Smart Shopper Lab
goal: Your kid makes a real purchase decision: something they're buying with their own money, or something the family needs. They compare two options, build their own scoring rubric, see both in person if they can, work out what each really costs, spot the marketing tricks, then wait before buying. The point is the habit of stopping and thinking before spending.
need: A real purchase coming up: something your kid is buying with their own money, or something the family needs
Paper and a pencil, or a notes app, and a calculator
A store to see both options, or a device to look up products, prices and reviews

lesson.text: The price tag isn't the real cost. Divide the price by how many times you'll use it, and the cheap option is often the expensive one.
lesson.before: The $5 water bottle is cheaper, obviously.

model.line: $30 bottle, used every day for a year: $30 ÷ 365 = about 8¢ per use.
$5 bottle, lost after a month: $5 ÷ 30 = about 17¢ per use.
The 'cheap' bottle costs twice as much every time you drink from it.
Buy A, if you'll really keep it. That 'if' is the honest part.

lesson.modelNote: Price tags hide how long a thing lasts. Cost per use counts that, plus the month the cheap bottle goes missing.

howTo.intro: The trap here is steering them toward the sensible choice. Let them pick something they actually want, keep your verdict to yourself, and treat 'I changed my mind' as a win: it means the process worked.

plan.what: Pick the two options, sort need or want and build the rubric (Steps 1 and 2).
See both, work out the true cost and spot the tricks (Steps 3 and 4).
Decide, buy it or don't, and set a date to check (Step 5).

troubleshoot.a: That's fine if they can explain it. The goal is a decision with reasons, not the cheapest choice.

troubleshoot.q: The rubric says the 'wrong' one won
troubleshoot.a: Perfect. Ask which score they'd change and why. That's where the real thinking happens.

skills.name: Cost thinking
skills.text: price per use, not price per tag

skills.name: Skepticism
skills.text: seeing the selling behind the product

steps.title: Pick two options to compare
steps.why: A real choice between two specific things, and a gut guess before the work.
steps.kid: Your kid picks something they're really about to buy: with their own money, as a gift, or something the family needs, like new shoes. Then they pick two specific options, like Brand A or Brand B, or the $20 version or the $45 version. They write: 'I'm comparing ___ and ___. My gut says I'd pick ___.'
steps.you: Help them pick a purchase that's actually coming up, so the decision counts. If they're stuck, offer two choices: 'Want to compare water bottles or headphones?' gets a faster answer than an open question.
ask: Which one do you think you'd pick right now?
Is this something you need or something you want?
steps.tip: Write the gut pick down and keep it. You'll come back to it in Step 5.

levels.explore: Pick a real thing you want and two options you can see or hold.
levels.develop: Look up two real options with prices, online or in a flyer.
levels.extend: Set a budget, predict the winner, and name the one fact that would flip your pick.

steps.title: Need or want, then build the rubric
steps.why: An honest label, and a scorecard built on what matters to them.
steps.kid: First, your kid decides: need or want? A need is something you can't really go without to stay warm, safe and fed, like a winter coat. A want is something you'd enjoy but could live without. Then they pick criteria (price, quality, reviews, features, style, how long it lasts) and draw a rubric: criteria down the side, both options across the top, a score from 1 to 5 in every box.
steps.you: Ask questions, don't judge. If colour matters more than durability to them, let the rubric show the trade-off. Watch for the moment a 'need' turns out to be a 'want.'
ask: If you could only check two things before buying, what would they be?
What would make you return it after a week?
steps.tip: Most purchases are wants dressed up as needs. That pause when they realise it is the whole lesson.

levels.explore: Need or want? Pick 3 things that matter and tick the winner of each.
levels.develop: Explain the need or want label, pick 5 criteria and rank them by importance.
levels.extend: Weight the top criteria double, then check: does changing one weight change the winner?

steps.title: See them, then work out the true cost
steps.why: What it's like in your hands, and what it really costs, not what the tag says.
steps.kid: If they can, your kid goes to see both options: holds them, tries them on, reads the box for what's included. Then they look past the sticker price three ways. Cost per use: price ÷ number of uses. Hidden costs: batteries, refills, accessories, shipping, a subscription. Opportunity cost: 'If I don't buy this, I could use the money for ___.' Then they update the rubric.
steps.you: Take them to the store if you can, and let them handle both. Help with the division if needed. Estimating uses is fine: about twice a week for a year is about 100 uses.
ask: What did you notice in person that the picture didn't show?
Which one is cheaper once you count how long it lasts?
steps.tip: Shoes that pinch, a lid that won't close, headphones that hurt after ten minutes: holding the thing settles more than any review.

levels.explore: Hold both and say one thing you'd only know in person. Then divide each price by its uses on a calculator.
levels.develop: See both if you can, add one hidden cost each, and name the opportunity cost.
levels.extend: Per month: $45 shoes lasting 12 months or $20 lasting 4? How long must the $45 pair last to win?

steps.title: Spot the marketing tricks
steps.why: Stop looking at the product. Look at the selling.
steps.kid: Your kid looks at how each option is sold (the product page, the box, the ad) and finds at least 3 tricks from the Marketing Tricks page at the end of the guide: urgency, fake scarcity, crossed-out prices, star counts, paid influencers, free shipping thresholds, 'you deserve this' language. Then they ask: did any of these sneak into my scores?
steps.you: Let them go down the rabbit hole. This step is the one they'll use for life.
ask: Is the product good, or is the marketing just good?
What would this page say with only facts?
steps.tip: Once kids start spotting tricks, they can't unsee them. Expect running commentary on every ad for a while. Worth it.

levels.explore: Spot 2 or 3 tricks across both options.
levels.develop: Spot 4 tricks and say which one almost worked on you.
levels.extend: Rewrite one product description with only facts, then list what the seller left out on purpose.

steps.title: Decide, wait, then buy
steps.why: A decision someone else could follow, and time to find out if it's real.
steps.kid: Your kid writes the pick in one sentence with the top reasons from the rubric and the true cost, and checks the gut pick from Step 1. Then the decision waits: two weeks for a want, a few days for a need. If they still want it, they buy it, with their own money if it's theirs, and put a date on the calendar a month later: do I still use it?
steps.you: Hold the wait, even if they beg. If the price drops or a bad review shows up during it, let them adjust: that's real information. Praise a changed mind out loud.
ask: What's the strongest reason for your pick?
Do you still want it as much as two weeks ago?
steps.tip: If they've forgotten about it by the end of the wait, they just saved money, and learned something no rubric could teach.

levels.explore: Tell me your pick and why in 3 sentences while I write, then wait a few days before buying.
levels.develop: Write the recommendation with rubric and cost evidence, wait two weeks, then decide.
levels.extend: Before buying, imagine it's a year later and the purchase was a mistake. Write what went wrong, and check if your pick survives it.

reference.title: Marketing Tricks
reference.intro: How products get sold to you. Find at least 3 in Step 4. Most ads use more than one at once.

items.name: Pressure

lines.v: 'Limited edition' that never really runs out
a deal that's back next week
'Sale ends in 02:14:37' ticking on the page

items.ask: Ask yourself: would I still want it if the deal were here next month?

items.name: Proof

lines.v: someone famous, often paid to say it
a badge that doesn't say who decided
a fun video that's really an ad

items.ask: Ask yourself: who is saying this, and do they get paid if I buy?

lines.v: 'Buy 2, get 1 free' when you only needed one

items.ask: Ask yourself: what is the real price of the thing I actually need?

lines.v: 'Upgrade now' when the old one still works
smiling kids, sunny days, friends laughing

items.ask: Ask yourself: am I buying the thing or the feeling in the picture?

after.label: Before you buy: the 3-question check
lines: 1. Is this a need or a want?
2. What does it cost per use, not just at the till?
3. Will I still want it in two weeks?

conclusion.headline: They check cost per use now, not just the tag.
conclusion.text: At the store, hold up two versions of something you buy, like two packs of batteries, and ask which is the better deal. Listen for 'how long does it last?' before 'which is cheaper?' If that question comes first, the cost-per-use maths stuck.
conclusion.celebrate: Repeat back the number that decided it: 'So the $45 pair is cheaper per month. That's going to change how I shop too.'
extensions: Run the rubric on the next big family purchase
Compare three options instead of two
Keep a list of every marketing trick you spot for a week
When someone says 'I need this,' do the need or want check out loud together

signs: They ask how long something will last before buying
They point out crossed-out prices and countdown timers
They say 'let me wait a few days' about something they want
makeItReal: Make the two-week wait a family rule for any want over a set amount, like $20, with the date on a sticky note on the fridge.
levelsLine: Every step has three levels: Explore, Develop, Extend. Pick the one that fits your kid today, and change it anytime. Siblings can do the same step at different levels, side by side.

fromHome.text: My son went back and forth between a Switch 2 and a PS5. The Switch 2 was cheaper, but that's not what decided it. It had more of the games he loves, and it travels with us, which matters a lot right now since we're on the road all the time. He picked the one that fit how he actually lives.
